book: 090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know

chapters.relation: Richard Greene uses Dracula's transformations (man, bat, wolf, mist, and human-to-vampire) plus Vlad the Impaler's ordinary aging to pose the puzzle of persistence: the claims of consistency, change, and persistence cannot all be true together. He raises the justice objection to mereological essentialism (if any change made Vlad a new person, imprisoning him would punish someone else) and then tests endurantism (wholly present with time-indexed properties), perdurantism (temporal parts), and exdurantism (temporal counterparts) against the Count. He concludes endurantism best captures the intuition that one and the same guy was first human and later vampire.

Versteeg and Barkman use Dracula's shapeshifting to stage Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?': even if the Count becomes a bat, whatever he recalls afterward is filtered back through his human-ness, so no non-bat can access bat-ness from a human point of view. A scene of Van Helsing and bat-Dracula both finding a girl's corpse distinguishes objective from subjective experience. Because physicalism predicts all of reality should be objectively accessible, the impenetrability of subjective experience pressures physicalism and leaves room for the immaterial soul Van Helsing's religion wants.

Karavitis applies Walter Benjamin's 'Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' to his own deflated re-reading of Dracula: mass reproduction stripped the novel of its ritual aura, and film (stage Lugosi versus screen Lugosi) made art analyzable, political, and economically driven. He reads Stoker's epistolary form and Mina's surviving transcription - the originals destroyed - as heralding a postmodern world where every viewpoint is equally valid, so each reader's gaze (feminist, Marxist, Blacula, Count Chocula) remakes the Count. A closing dialectic moves from passive contemplation (thesis) through critical reading (antithesis) to readers becoming authors themselves (synthesis).

De Waal reads Dracula through Judith Butler's gender performativity: the Count terrifies because he 'does' gender wrong - a captor who cooks and mothers Jonathan like an 'angel in the house,' feeds Mina from his breast, and turns Lucy from Victorian maiden into wanton vamp. Harker as a 'dude in distress,' Van Helsing's hysteria, and the Dracula-Mina scene that 'opens new orifices' become parodies exposing gender as an incessant citation of copies. The hunters' 'sterilizing' of Dracula's boxes of earth is read against the eugenics movement and society's police function against gender-nonconforming people.

Tim Jones uses Jung's Shadow to argue Dracula is the British Empire's Shadow Self: everything the Count does in Britain - draining resources, reshaping native identities - mirrors what Britain does abroad, minus the benevolent veneer, while Ego-projection explains why Harker's crew must annihilate him rather than admit what he reflects. The chapter adds that colonial stereotypes became self-fulfilling, with colonized peoples made to live the imposed identities, and reads the era's reverse-invasion fiction (mummies, The War of the Worlds) as a collective staking of the Shadow. It closes by recommending Jungian ownership of the Shadow instead of projection.

Pötzsch reads Dracula through Freud's Civilization and Its Discontents: the Count fascinates because he lives out the aggression and sexual freedom civilization forces us to renounce, embodying the innate hostility in Freud's 'man is the wolf to man.' Freud's account - group power replacing individual might, 'love thy neighbor' as an impossible demand, the super-ego as an inner Van Helsing breeding guilt over forbidden impulses, with the id and ego mediating - is mapped onto Jonathan's 'wicked, burning desire' for the vampire women. The upshot: we resent culture because we traded happiness for security, yet living like Dracula would get our throats cut.

Callis reads the 1931 Lugosi film through Jung: Dracula is Mina's Shadow archetype and animus, embodying her repressed fear of sexuality and of the married life she claims to want, while the vampire's presence in every culture places him in the collective unconscious. Mina's arc - the Call to Adventure, crossing the threshold into Dracula's embrace, and 'resurrection' after his staking - becomes a Shero's Journey of confronting the shadow, with Dracula also playing the Shapeshifter archetype. The chapter ends doubting the happy ending, asking whether Mina defeated her shadow or merely surrendered her dreams of freedom.

Karavitis fabricates a recovered 'Dracula's Journal' in which the Count retells Stoker's plot as rational self-interest: he owes no one anything, Lucy 'came to me of her own free will,' Van Helsing's crew are a 'craven collective' spouting 'from each according to his ability,' and only objective reality - not their subjective feelings - counts. He claims a fundamental right to pursue his own happiness, casting himself as the thinking individual crushed by proletarian herd morality. An editor's framing email makes the point explicit: Rand-style egoism could justify even Dracula, a 'manual for vampires' set against Marx's collectivism.

In imaginary letters, Meursault of Camus's The Stranger describes his meaning-free life, his trial that condemned his refusal to perform feelings, and his death-row move from indifference to acceptance of the absurd, then inducts Dracula into Camus's gallery of absurd heroes beside Don Juan, Don Quixote, and Sisyphus - those who reject suicide, reject help from higher powers, and accept life's absurdity. Dracula accepts the first two traits but categorically rejects despairing acceptance, claiming love and conquest instead. An appendix lets Sisyphus himself grumble that Camus finding happiness in boulder-pushing is the real absurdity.

Ketcham's invented chronicle sends Dracula and a village rabbi to 1194 Cairo to interrogate Maimonides: can resurrection - one of the thirteen principles of faith - apply to a soulless undead being, and is his blood-drinking a divinely imposed penance? Maimonides answers from the Guide for the Perplexed and the Letter on Resurrection, offering that intelligence is the essence of the soul yet judging the Count a likely trickster, while Dracula presses that no scientific evidence of dust becoming flesh exists. The diarist closes with the heretical worry that Maimonidean resurrection - no food, drink, or sex - might itself be a kind of undeath.

Sexton's mock FBI COMPIC file stages a Cold War reading of Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein: screenwriters Lees and Rinaldo remake Dracula as Marx's Das Kapital vampire - capital as dead labour sucking living labour - so blood-draining becomes profit-draining and 'This man belongs to me!' the capitalist's claim on his workers. A fictional Ayn Rand review for HUAC decodes the film as collectivist propaganda that slanders the businessman McDougal and dreams of a creature with 'no will of his own,' touching Marxian alienation along the way. A final note links screenwriter Robert Lees's blacklisting by Sterling Hayden and his real-life decapitation to Stoker's vampire-killing instructions.

holes.name: Persistence Through Change (endurantism vs perdurantism)
holes.what: The debate over how objects persist through time: enduring wholly present at each moment, perduring as sums of temporal parts, or persisting via temporal counterparts.
holes.why: Chapter 24 is built entirely on this trilemma of consistency, change, and persistence and evaluates endurantism, perdurantism, and exdurantism against Dracula's shapeshifting, which the generic 'personal-identity' slug does not cover.

holes.name: Roland Barthes
holes.what: French literary theorist whose 'death of the author' holds that a text's meaning is made by readers, not fixed by authorial intention.
holes.why: Chapter 27 explicitly invokes Barthes to argue that mechanically reproduced Dracula turns every reader into an author who decides what the novel says.

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Mythologist whose monomyth, the Hero's Journey, describes the universal arc of the call to adventure, threshold crossing, ordeal, and return.
holes.why: Chapter 31 structures Mina's confrontation with Dracula as a 'Shero's Journey' using Campbell's Call to Adventure and the stages of the hero's transformation.

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Novelist-philosopher of Objectivism, which holds rational self-interest as the moral ideal and rejects obligation to the collective.
holes.why: Chapter 33 ventriloquizes Dracula's diary as a Randian defense of egoism and objective reality against Van Helsing's Marxist 'collective herd'.

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Novelist-philosopher of Objectivism, which holds rational self-interest as the moral ideal and rejects obligation to the collective.
holes.why: Chapter 36 stages Ayn Rand's fictional HUAC review decoding Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein as collectivist propaganda against capitalism.
